#9105. Barbara Takenaga’s ‘Awestruck’

At Kemper Museum of Contemporary Art, 40 paintings invite viewers into an exhibition where scale, pattern, and perception are explored and celebrated.

On view at Kemper Museum of Contemporary Art in Kansas City through April 11, 2027, Barbara Takenaga: Awestruck presents the artist’s first comprehensive survey in nearly a decade. Bringing together 40 works spanning her career since the early 2000s, the exhibition reveals the many approaches to abstraction that have shaped Takenaga’s practice. The exhibition is organized by Jessica May, Ph.D., Executive Director, Kemper Museum of Contemporary Art, and Tae Edell, Independent Curator.

The exhibition examines Barbara Takenaga’s intricate compositions through four thematic sections: an emphasis on process, a masterful confusion of scale, an embrace of illusion, and reverent nods to art history. Together, these strategies work to upend the viewer’s expectations, engaging imagination and stoking curiosity for more.

Featuring works from institutional and private collections across the nation, this exhibition includes paintings up to her most recent, revealing Takenaga’s continued push to further her approach across increasingly expanding canvases, opening new paths within her ongoing exploration of abstraction.

Learn more and plan your visit at kemperart.org.

#9104. Life mirrors art: the story of Yayoi Kusama

Kusama in the first of her signature Infinity Room pieces, Infinity Mirror Room—Phalli’s Field (1965) at Castellane Gallery, New York © Yayoi Kusama

When Yayoi Kusama died in Tokyo on 14 August, aged 97, she left behind a legacy almost unparalleled in contemporary art. The Japanese artist, who arrived in New York in 1958 as an outsider—female, Asian and largely unknown—eventually became one of the most recognisable artists on the planet. Her dots and pumpkins migrated from canvases and sculptures onto handbags and shopfronts; her Infinity Mirror Rooms generated queues around museums and millions of selfies.

Yet Kusama’s visibility has, when it comes to the structures that once excluded her, remained extraordinary.

“Kusama’s global success has had enormous symbolic force,” says Izumi Nakajima, an art historian specialising in feminism and post-war Japanese art. “Yet the exceptional success of an individual woman artist and a structural transformation in the gendered and geographical asymmetries of the art world operate on different registers.” A canon, Nakajima adds, can accommodate “a small number of monumental women artists while continuing to marginalise a far larger number of women”.

That distinction complicates the familiar story of Kusama as a trailblazer for women and Asian artists. Japan in the 1950s and early 60s, Nakajima says, had a substantial cohort of women pursuing experimental practices, including Atsuko Tanaka and Hideko Fukushima. To project Kusama’s present fame backwards risks producing a history in which she appears uniquely radical from the outset. Kusama’s departure from Japan in 1957 was crucial: while Japan’s high-growth era increasingly reorganised women’s lives around domesticity, she pursued her career abroad, relentlessly making both her art and herself visible through exhibitions, photographs, fashion, happenings and the media.

For the Tokyo- and Vienna-based feminist and queer publishing and research collective Multiple Spirits, the transformation since Kusama’s early career is nevertheless real. Compared with a global art world then dominated overwhelmingly by white men, opportunities to encounter artists from different backgrounds have unquestionably expanded, the collective says. But it questions whether Kusama’s trajectory should still function as a model of “success” when the criteria by which success is measured remain largely inherited from that same art world. “Values and measures different from those shaped by a white male-centred art world are still insufficient,” the collective says.

Nor does Nakajima see Kusama fitting comfortably into another role frequently assigned to her: that of the feminist icon. Rather than treating feminism as “an attribute or categorical designation”, Nakajima argues, it is more productive to use it as a critical method through which to read her work. Kusama’s repetition, sexuality, self-representation and negotiation of the body all invite feminist interpretation. But unlike strands of feminist art that rejected Modernism’s claims to autonomy and universality, Kusama repeatedly resisted being circumscribed as either a “woman” or a “Japanese” artist. “She sought to occupy the position of the universal artistic subject that Modernism had imagined,” Nakajima says.

The Multiple Spirits collective similarly notes a gap between Kusama’s international reception and her popular image at home. In Japan, it says, she is less commonly understood as a feminist icon than as the creator of colourful polka-dotted paintings and installations. The politics of her 1960s happenings—their anti-war messages and calls for sexual liberation—have received comparatively less attention. Rather than reducing Kusama to an individual “feminist” or “queer” identity, the collective argues that these radical practices need to be reconsidered within the social and cultural conditions that produced them.

Another paradox lies in Kusama’s transformation from avant-garde provocateur to global cultural brand. In 1966, she appeared uninvited at the Venice Biennale with Narcissus Garden, offering mirrored spheres for sale beneath a sign declaring “Your Narcissism for Sale”. Decades later, the mirrors themselves became among contemporary art’s most coveted attractions. Visitors queue for hours to spend seconds inside an Infinity Mirror Room, phone in hand, while collaborations with Louis Vuitton turned her dots into a globally recognisable luxury motif. Critics have consequently cast Kusama as both a precursor of the immersive “artainment” economy and one of its most successful brands.

For Hidenori Ota, the founder of the gallery Ota Fine Arts and Kusama’s longtime representative in Japan, the artist’s embrace of visibility cannot be separated from the struggle to make herself heard. “I imagine that, in order to deliver a voice that otherwise could not reach people, she first needed to make her own presence larger,” he says. Having directly experienced war, Ota suggests, Kusama sought a language capable of reaching a mass audience, repeatedly returning to the word “love” as a vehicle for criticism.

Kusama and a life-size replica, from her collaboration with Louis Vuitton © Yayoi Kusama

Kusama’s popularity also made mental illness unusually visible within mainstream contemporary art. She voluntarily lived at a psychiatric hospital in Tokyo from 1977 onward, working for decades at a nearby studio. While frequently connecting her compulsive repetition and artistic production to hallucinations and psychological distress, she generally eschewed disability advocacy. Narratives around Kusama have drawn criticism for reproducing the familiar trope of the “mad genius” who triumphs over adversity, while doing relatively little to address disability, psychiatric experience or accessibility. Nakajima similarly warns against narratives that link women’s creativity to illness, trauma and psychological compulsion: such frameworks, she says, have historically helped women artists gain recognition while simultaneously restricting how their practices are understood.

Perhaps the most troubling asterisk in Kusama’s legacy relates to her descriptions of Black people in her 2002 autobiography, Infinity Net. In the original Japanese edition, she blamed Black residents and unhoused people for the decline of her New York neighbourhood. That, along with other denigrating lines, was omitted from the 2011 English translation. When the comments received renewed attention ahead of her 2023 exhibition at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, Kusama said she “deeply regret[ted] using hurtful and offensive language” and apologised for the pain she had caused.

The episode sits uneasily beside the universalist language of love that characterised Kusama’s later public persona. Asked how it should shape her legacy, Ota says: “Rather than simply viewing her through that label of ‘racist’, [her words] should be examined in relation to the social conditions and historical context of the time.” He adds that it requires further debate and study. The controversy nevertheless underscores the limits of transforming a complex historical figure into an uncomplicated symbol of inclusion.

Ota is likewise sceptical of attributing subsequent changes in Asia’s art world to a single artist. “Rather than Kusama changing things herself, I think the larger shifts of the era—particularly the social and economic rise of Asia—were more significant,” he says. “She moved in step with those larger changes.”

Kusama’s 1967 “happening”, Body Festival, in which polka dot-painted participants danced in public New York spaces © Yayoi Kusama

The Multiple Spirits collective flags how, in Japan and beyond, as shrinking cultural budgets require museums to pursue larger audiences and alternative funding sources, Kusama shows became reliable for producing economic results. But her visibility has not particularly helped other marginalised artists. “We cannot entrust structural change in the art world to the success story of a minority artist,” the collective says. What matters instead are less spectacular changes: improving working conditions and accessibility, using inclusive language, protecting freedom of expression and connecting such efforts across institutions.

Kusama entered a Western, male-dominated art world and ultimately became bigger than almost any artist within it. But “exceptional success and structural inequality can coexist”, Nakajima observes. Kusama changed who could occupy the centre of contemporary art, but not the nature of that centre.

Why Club Nothing (R) is more than empty philanthropy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Tech brand Nothing has a rare upper hand that few of its rivals can claim – it is, I dare say, pretty cool. Already, the words 'brand' and 'cool' together irk me a bit; it feels antithetical to say a company trying to sell you things could ever truly be 'cool', but somehow Nothing has carved an identity that feels real, and I've been sucked right in.

From its trend-defying product design to its slick campaigns, Nothing oozes style in an effortless way that many brands will spend an eternity trying to capture. Sometimes it's not about competing for the best adverts or the swankiest product launches, but building something authentic.

Nothing has been on my radar for a while, particularly after it employed 365 party girl Charli XCX to promote its Headphone model. Nothing came out swinging, announcing Charli as its first Global Brand Ambassador, marking a distinct finger on the pulse of pop culture. With a Midas touch for all things cool, getting the BRAT composer to be the face of its brand was an instant boost in social clout.

But Nothing doesn't just embrace this party lifestyle as a fleeting trend. The return of its Club Nothing (R) initiative sees the brand support grassroots music scenes, underground parties, and alternative sound experiences with a $40,000 grant. This year's winners, Black Bass Collective, Oroko Radio, Whorechata and Signal, represent a diverse array of independent music culture, providing a much-needed boost for the struggling and uncertain status of the live music scene.

In short, Nothing's 'cool' image isn't just performative; it's productive. Often, brand philanthropy can come across as virtue signalling, but Nothing knows its place in culture and is actively helping to improve the industry that supports it. Being cool is much more than getting the latest trending celeb to rep your tech – it's about living and breathing community.

For more Nothing news, check out why Nothing designs its phones “like logos” or take a look at why the Nothing Phone (4b) makes no sense, but we still love it.

#9102. Nuart Aberdeen 2026: Poetry In The Streets

Welcome to the latest edition of Nuart Aberdeen. As far as we can ascertain, this will be the first street art festival in the world with a focus primarily on poetry and text-based works. Over the years, for better or worse, the large scale colourful figurative mural has come to dominate the culture we work with, and although it’s an aspect of the culture we support, due to the resources required to produce murals, they’re perhaps also the least democratic form of art on the streets. As curators, researchers and producers working in “festival” culture, we have a responsibility to not only showcase and celebrate the most interesting and technically competent works of our time, but to also ensure the culture’s development and survival. The only way to do this, is to inspire and encourage those without the privilege of a fine art degree or access to the arts, to have a go themselves. This has always been Nuart’s primary goal, not just to produce art, but to also inspire and produce the next generation of artists. A lofty goal, particularly as it’s often in conflict with the stated needs of sponsors and partners, on paper at least, and no one stands in front of a Tower block mural and thinks, I’ll pop home and have a go myself on the gable end of Gran’s house.

What we do have evidence for, is that the smaller, more human scale works – the stencils and paste ups and interventions – do have this effect. You could say that the ease of copying a Banksy stencil, which requires no more than a craft knife, a piece of cardboard and an idea, is the very foundation of this culture. We’ve seen this happen time and time again. Indeed, several of the producers and artists joining us this year, started their artistic journey as assistants and volunteers at Nuart.

At Nuart, we’ve always prided ourselves on not only showcasing the BIG names in muralism, but on also using the festival as a place to explore and experiment with new forms and ideas that engage with the idea of the whole city as a canvas, and not just the wall. In this respect, Nuart Aberdeen have been fortunate enough to have the support of some of the most thoughtful and progressive partners that an event such as Nuart could possibly have, and this year is no different.

Whilst pondering this issue, how to balance the needs of partners, tourist boards, with the need to impress the public, and create works of curiosity and interest for scholars which inspire the next generation, I imagined a city without art on the streets, with no forms of public expression, where all art is concealed behind the walls of city institutions and under guard 24/7. And then I recalled a piece of graffiti sprayed on the walls of Paris during the 1968 student uprising, an event which saw waves of creative energy explode onto the streets. It read, “La poésie est dans la rue”, or “Poetry is in the Streets” – could we harness some of this energy at Nuart to revitalise and energise the culture?

A short while later, I remembered a quote from pioneering UK graffiti writer Mode2. He was discussing how graffiti culture had taken hold and blossomed in the UK in the 1980s, and in a throwaway quip had said, the reason it took hold was because regardless of how interested you were in making art at school, if you couldn’t draw or paint realistically, you were bottom of the class. Then graffiti came along, and it struck everyone that all you had to know to create and engage with it, was your ABC’s.

And that was it. It was these two quite innocuous events that formed the genesis of this year’s poetry and text based Nuart. These are forms of creative expression that we all have access to and I hope the festival sparks the public’s imagination in the same way that those early bubble letters and Banksy stencils did.

Thank you as ever to all of our sponsors, partners and to the city council, for allowing us once again to make a contribution to what we believe is a magical and inspiring city.

— Martyn Reed, Nuart Founder and CuratorArtists include: Alisa Oleva (UK) Ciarán Glöbel (SCT) dr.d AKA Subvertiser (UK) HICKS (UK) James Klinge (SCT) KMG (SCT) Molly Hankinson (UK) Remi Rough (UK) Robert Montgomery (SCT) The Rebel Bear (SCT) The Writing Is On The Wall (UK) Trackie McLeod (SCT)  V2k | (LT - SCT)

Christopher Glass discusses working on Boots Riley’s absurdist crime comedy.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Boots Riley's absurdist crime comedy I Love Boosters is far from conventional. From its stunning movie posters to its action-packed trailer, it's not a movie that comes quietly. Following a group of shoplifters as they face off against fashion mogul Christie Smith, the film soon spirals into a surreal science fiction body horror with some slicing social commentary for good measure.

But such an eccentric story needs immersive production design to match – that's where Christopher Glass comes in. To understand the meticulous practical effects process behind I Love Boosters and more, I sat down with Christopher to uncover the intricate artistry of production design and the evolution of the industry.

Christopher Glass is an Art Director Guild (ADG) Award-winning and Gold Cannes Lion-winning Production Designer whose work spans feature films, television, and commercials. Known for creating visually ambitious, emotionally resonant worlds - he has collaborated with some of the most influential directors working in film and advertising today.

I think beyond the obvious technological changes that have happened in the last 25 years (iPhones, iPads, Motion Capture/LED Volumes, real-time rendering and now AI) the largest conditions that have changed in the industry are economic.

The decentralization of film work from a Los Angeles hub to being scattered all over the world, chasing the latest tax rebate; the creation of IP-obsessed streaming platforms with tech companies swallowing traditional studios via ever larger mergers and acquisitions have created an environment where there is less work in general.

When there is work, it tends to be less creative and completely risk-averse. There is a focus on collecting libraries of “content” versus actually having an interest in making great films, TV shows or commercials. That’s why movies like “I Love Boosters” and what NEON and A24 are doing is much needed today.

In an ideal world, film companies would break away from these monstrous corporations and return to smaller autonomous studios, run by people who truly care about telling unique and compelling stories.

I think miniatures and forced perspective are my favorite practical effects, overlooked not only by audiences but also by filmmakers themselves. Filmmakers sometimes don’t know or realize these are great options for getting tangible effects in camera.

People tend to think miniatures have to be small buildings and cars. I have used 70% scale miniature “backings” to eliminate the need for LED walls or traditional translight backings. You get parallax when you move the camera. You can dress or light up windows how you want and change everything in modular ways. You can design sets with forced perspective to make things look further away or more expansive. These are techniques that have been around for over 100 years.

We used miniatures on “I Love Boosters” in a different way. Almost the entire third act is a combination of full-scale and 1/6th and 1/12th scale miniatures. We have stop-motion characters running across moving vehicles, down streets and alleys. It was an intentional choice for the handmade look.

In fact, when we were shooting, our Director Boots Riley thought some of the miniature shots started looking too real and told the folks at Blind Beagle FX (the miniature company run by Christopher Warren) to make them look more “miniature.”

I have a few favorite projects for varying reasons. “I Love Boosters” stands out for sure. Its sheer madness and creativity are unparalleled for me. I also really loved doing the battlefield war sets for “12 Strong” – which was a completely different experience – and “The Jungle Book” will always be a special film for me. I learned a hell of a lot from that and really loved the people I worked with.

Hands down, the Apple short film directed by Spike Jonze starring FKA Twigs called “Welcome Home.” Every detail, from the lighting, camera, props, actor choreography, music cues, and artwork, was subject to complicated practical effects and moving set pieces.

As an example, we built the apartment twice. One was “normal” and unmoving. The other one was the magic trick set where everything moved and stretched. Each moving piece affected the next, like a domino effect.

One time Spike asked me to move the coffee table about 4 inches in one direction. I had to explain to him that the metal table, with a spring-loaded stretching magazine was attached to the stretching rug, and both were bolted into moving tracks underneath the floor connected to levers hidden just out of view of the perpendicularly moving walls at the end of the room… So it wouldn’t be easy.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Everything in that set depended on precise placement, choreography and movement. Every pattern and texture of fabric had to be precisely made and printed to achieve the “pixel” stretching effect throughout. The umbrella on a stand, a bike and a lamp had to be meticulously sculpted to be extruded by movement.

The large moving wall actually hovered on air bearings and was timed to the music. The hallway was made of ribbons stretched with so much tension, it bent the original steel frame and had to be rebuilt before shooting. The list goes on and on. Nothing was easy about that project. I thought it was the end of my career, and it was all going to go down in flames. But to my pleasant surprise, we won a Gold Cannes Lion for Film Craft.

Coming in close second for most difficult was “I Love Boosters!”

#9099. Cinga Samson "Ukuphuthelwa" @ White Cube Gallery, NYC

South African artist Cinga Samson’s exhibition of new paintings is titled ‘Ukuphuthelwa’, an isiXhosa word in the artist’s native language that translates as ‘unable to sleep’. Unlike the English word ‘insomnia’, the isiXhosa term carries no negative connotation and accordingly, for Samson, sleeplessness is not a condition to be cured but a state of spiritual alertness, a sensitivity that deepens in the dark. Rendered in the artist’s signature occluded palette of near-blacks, carbon and deep Prussian blues, Samson’s scenes depict men-like figures, dogs in overgrown fields and portraits of plant life native to South Africa. Encouraging slow, contemplative looking, a sense of existential gravity pervades Samson’s new series of oil paintings, attempting to depict a vast reality that is continuously in motion. As the artist has it, his quandary pertains to the existential question of how to create a ‘true and honest painting'. The exhibition will be on view through April 18, 2026.

With ‘Ukuphuthelwa’, Samson considers his role as an artist in relation to his inability to represent the whole truth of reality, and the fact that he can merely make symbols. Between the static, painted sign and the fluid experience it gestures towards, he contends that there exists a gulf that no image can close. Though the technical mastery and convincing realism of these paintings appear to invite interpretation, the artist asserts that his work confronts the very dilemma of representation: that the image can only ever be a relative symbol of what it reflects, never its equivalent. Acknowledging the open-ended nature of symbols and their subjective interpretation, Samson takes the figure of the dog as an example. The viewer may, for instance, look at Intsingiselo II (2026) and perceive the loyalty conventionally associated with dogs, while an amaXhosa understanding might highlight the dog as signifying the guiding, protective principles of ancestors. Comprising painstaking detail and deft brushwork, Samson’s paintings do not disguise the limits of representation but, rather, aspire to harness his skills towards that which exceeds the representable. Above all, the artist’s work seeks out the authority of the unnameable and the territory of the sublime, one in which the divine is not found elsewhere but present in the vernacular of all things.

Samson’s larger compositions carry a palpable sense of reverence and ceremony. In Umlindo (Watcher) (2026), figures are gathered in a forest clearing with wildflower bouquets and lengths of fabric, a scene that carries the visual grammar of ritual without specifying its addressee or terms. For Samson however, ‘the ritual itself is not the important thing – it’s an opening to what exists beyond’, and the paintings use the aesthetics of ritual to speak to a collective need for orientation, as well as the capacity of ritual to mediate an encounter with a vast unknown. That the works are titled with enigmatic words and phrases in isiXhosa, such as Imfihlo (Secret) and Intsingiselo (Meaning) (both 2026), infer the same problem the paintings contend with – the instability of interpretation as it pertains to the knowable and unknowable. Each word carries a weight in isiXhosa that its English translation approaches but can never fully reach; here, just as between the painted sign and living referent, meaning slips between the interstice of two languages.

The objects, people and settings that recur in these paintings and across Samson’s oeuvre are identifiable and quotidian, yet Samson corrals in each an unexplained mystery. In Tshee (2026), a vast field stretches out, the silhouetted trees meeting a murky sky, though the void of the night is interrupted by a moonwashed cloud, its brilliant white destabilising the eerie, cold atmosphere suffused with majesty. ‘The sky can be so friendly, but sometimes so heavy, dark, so scary. It’s the same energy, but it exists in different forms’, Samson notes, conjuring an oscillation between the approachable and the overwhelming that recalls the affective register of the sublime. Sithini ngelilitye (2026), distils the same sensation: a rocky crag emerges from arid undergrowth, its surface rendered in forensic detail against a sky of barely-there wash, charging the scene with the same quality of mute enormity.

Marshalling light ‘like a magic trick’, Samson imparts a unique kind of rhythm to his paintings – a flickering that emerges and disperses across the picture plane, granting varying degrees of visibility to the dark, nighttime scenes. Producing an unsteadiness that is at once optical and psychical, the artist leaves large sections of the painting’s under-drawing visible to lend moments of transparency to the work. In Isiganeko (2026), for example, thin layers of glaze are applied and wiped back in his typical style, a means of building colour that lends the figures a brooding chromatic density, whilst elsewhere, in the undergrowth and the bird caught mid-flight, the under-drawing is left entirely exposed. In all Samson’s figures, the pupils of the eyes are left unpainted and allow ‘light’ to further circulate, a decision that renders them porous, so they are ‘completely one with the whole painting’. Without pupils, these figures are not personified identities, but ‘human’ forms enmeshed with the painting’s landscape and atmosphere, no element ever possessing full mastery over the other. In places where the ‘trick’ of painting reveals itself, it is as if Samson’s works were stepping back from the pretence or promise of representation. What ‘Ukuphuthelwa’ reaches towards is not individual transcendence in subordination, but rather the mystery that can be unearthed in ordinary forms, whose immanent magic is available to those who are sensitive to it. This is the condition that ‘Ukuphuthelwa’ ultimately describes: not an absence or deficit, but a hypersensitivity that affords everything in existence the same potential for eliciting wonder or fear. Samson’s pupilless figures do not ‘look’ outward because the figures’ knowing comes from within the world they inhabit, a shared knowledge that exists between the bowing foliage, the vigilant dog, the bird in flight and the foreboding of the night sky enshrouding them all. In Samson’s hands, each optical device and representational motif prises apart what it cannot contain, in service of painting ‘a thing that links us to God – by God, I mean everything’.

The most entertaining bit of game marketing I've seen in a long time.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Rockstar has found a brilliantly left-field way to show off Grand Theft Auto VI: by smuggling new footage into South Park. It’s one of the smartest bits of brand placement I’ve seen in a long time but its also just the right kind of unexpected disruption I'd expect from Rockstar.

Game marketing usually runs on slick trailers and carefully managed hype. A dog poo weapon demo inside a crudely animated cartoon is the opposite of that, but it works. The latest episode of South Park (or is it South America now?), ‘Guinea Pig on a Stick’, aired on 28 October and included around 20 seconds of previously unseen gameplay from the forthcoming open-world game, GTA 6.

The clip follows protagonists Jason and Lucia along a busy Vice City beach before switching to Jason, who spots a dog doing its business on the sand. The owner dutifully bags the mess, but Jason has other ideas. He throws something at the hapless dog walker, grabs the bag of poo and smacks the NPC round the face with it. Charming.

New gameplay from GTA 6 was shown in the latest ‘SOUTH PARK’ episode. https://t.co/gL2kRKUv2IOctober 29, 2026

The visual clash is half the fun. South Park’s flat, cut-out look has barely changed in decades, and dropping a few seconds of Rockstar’s richly detailed, near-photoreal world into it makes the game’s fidelity stand out more than another polished trailer would. The footage is the real thing, too, with Rockstar Games credited in the closing credits.

From a branding point of view, it’s a refreshing move. GTA 6 is the biggest entertainment release of the year, if not the decade, and Rockstar could simply keep releasing bigger trailers and let the internet amplify them (having begun with an equally unique Netflix reveal). Instead, it’s placing the game inside a piece of pop culture that already has an audience, and a voice, of its own.

It’s in keeping with a campaign that has been playful from the start, from a neon logo that reads as a love letter to Vice City and box art that leans hard into PS2-era nostalgia to cheeky parody ads that blur reality and fiction on the streets of Miami.

It also doesn’t feel like an ad. South Park has been referencing GTA 6 all season, so the appearance lands as a punchline rather than a paid slot. Both brands trade on irreverence and a willingness to go further than their rivals, so the tone matches. Nothing feels forced. That’s more than can be said for the brands trying to borrow the Vice City look, from Burger King to Shrek. Rockstar keeps official tie-ups tightly controlled, and the Miami Heat’s Vice City merchandise is a rare example.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

There’s a nice bit of brand history here, too. The narrator of the gameplay footage is voiced by Tish Hicks, who also provided the voiceover for GTA 5’s official gameplay video back in 2013. It’s a small touch, but it’s the kind of consistency that makes a brand feel coherent over time, and longtime fans will spot it.

What I like most is that Rockstar is letting a comedy show poke fun at one of its biggest selling points: the extraordinary detail of its worlds. That apparently includes weaponising dog mess.

With GTA 6 due on 19 November, there’s still time for more surprises. If this is the template, I’d take it over another dozen predictable cinematic trailers.

#9097. Ana Mendieta's Lasting Imprint on Art

A major survey at Tate Modern asks us to take notice of the earth, the power of the female body, and the artist’s remarkable practice.

LONDON — Barely there but deftly constructed, Ana Mendieta’s Siluetas could be anywhere. Some are almost invisible in her documentary photographs. In one from 1979, a human form is impressed into the mud among similar natural shapes on a dried-out riverbank. In another from 1978, a few shimmering leaves, flowers, and branches sketch out the ghost of a woman against a dark tree trunk. Ana Mendieta, a major survey exhibition at Tate Modern, however, asks us to take notice: of the earth, the power of the female body, and the artist’s remarkable practice.

The exhibition eschews a chronological approach, opting to organize works according to their physical and metaphorical places, such as The Grove, The School, or The Sacred Grounds. This effectively points visitors towards the essential site-specificity of Mendieta’s practice; individual works are made in dialogue with particular locations of personal, ecological, or spiritual significance. More broadly, as the wall text explains, Mendieta described her practice as an “attempt to return to the maternal source,” in response to being “cast from the womb (Nature)” through her exile from Cuba as a child.

The exhibition opens with “The Cave,” featuring late works from the 1980s, including her very last video piece “Ochún” (1981) and a selection of her “rupestrian” sculptures inspired by prehistoric rock art. Whereas her more famous Silueta series generally features an imprint or silhouette of Mendieta’s own body, these lesser-known later works are more open-ended in style. Here, female forms are borrowed not from the artist’s anatomy but from the natural forms of rocks and prehistoric representations of goddesses.

#9096. Documenta 16 hires four new curators

Left to right: Osei Bonsu, Raven Chacon, Noam Segal and Timea Junghaus

Bonsu: © Gas Foundation; Chacon: © Neal Santos; Segal: © Samantha Casolari; Junghaus: © Zoltan Adam

The curatorial team for Documenta 16 is expanding with the announcement of four new appointments. The new team members are the composer and installation artist Raven Chacon, who was named curator-at-large, alongside the curators and art historians Osei Bonsu, Timea Junghaus and Noam Segal, who were appointed curatorial advisers.

The next edition of the influential quinquennial contemporary art exhibition, which will take place next year (12 June-19 September) in Kassel, is led by Naomi Beckwith, the deputy director and chief curator of the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum.

Her team of four women curators—Carla Acevedo-Yates, Romi Crawford, Mayra A. Rodríguez Castro, and Xiaoyu Weng—will develop the exhibition, publications and programming for the upcoming edition.

The artistic team for documenta 16: Romi Crawford, Mayra A. Rodríguez Castro, Xiaoyu Weng, Carla Acevedo-Yates, and Naomi Beckwith

© documenta and Museum Fridericianum gGmbH / Photo: Nicolas Wefers

Chacon unveiled the two-mile-long land art installation Repellent Fence at the US/Mexico border in 2015; in 2022, he became the first Indigenous artist to be awarded the Pulitzer Prize for Music. Bonsu is senior curator of international art, Africa, and diaspora at Tate Modern, where he co-curated Nigerian Modernism in 2025.

Junghaus was the founding director of Gallery8 – Roma Contemporary Art Space in Budapest (2013–2017) and launched the European Roma Institute for Arts and Culture in Berlin in 2017. Segal serves as the LG Electronics associate curator at the Guggenheim Museum in New York and was previously the director of curatorial research in the Master’s programme for curatorial practice at the School of Visual Arts, New York.

According to an online statement, “the [Documenta 16] exhibition and programmes will honour artists as they navigate a world in turmoil, developing strategies and new possibilities for living together amid planetary indeterminacy. Improvisation, experimentation, and collective learning will open new paths.”

The last edition of Documenta in 2022 sparked controversy after two antisemitic images were found in the work People’s Justice (2000), by the Indonesian artist collective, Taring Padi. The work was removed from show and, in the following days, Documenta posted a statement that was attributed to the Jakarta-based collective ruangrupa, who curated the exhibition. It read in part: “We acknowledge that this was our error.”

#9095. Sophia Huitema "Prussian Blue" @ Harper’s Apartment

Harper’s is pleased to announce Prussian Blue, New York–based artist Sophia Huitema’s first solo exhibition with the gallery. The presentation features new works by Huitema and will be on view through April 25, 2026.

Across the seven oil paintings on view, the visual and chemical properties of the pigment Prussian Blue function as a metaphorical anchor, tying together a cast of watchful female figures within Huitema’s hazy, dreamlike worlds. Working within a restrained range of blue and green tones, the paintings evoke a moody atmosphere through cool harmonies and dimly lit interiors. Prussian Blue, derived from chemical processes historically linked to cyanide while also used as an antidote to certain forms of poisoning, embodies a rare duality in which toxicity and protection converge, mirroring the emotionally guarded, ambiguous presence of Huitema’s figures.

The tension between beauty and menace permeates Huitema’s subjects. Elongated figures with exaggerated limbs and slender necks slink through each scene, often directly confronting the viewer’s gaze. Set within opulent surroundings that recall Gatsby–era decadence, Huitema’s women bear the markers of high society themselves, dressed in elegant gowns and adorned with pearl necklaces or jewel-studded headdresses. Moving through film-noir settings with poise and a quietly calculating air, these femme fatales seem either to lure their audience into a seductive ruse or to deploy their own cunning to evade danger. In Sleeper Car, for example, a woman fitted in a backless evening gown tilts her head slyly over her right shoulder in a relaxed pose while her right hand appears braced and ready to strike. As rain streaks across the coach’s windows and the narrow aisle stretches into an uncertain depth, a moment of cinematic suspense emerges, evoking the apex of a psychological thriller. In this way, Huitema constructs a world of heightened atmosphere and theatrical tension that opens onto the broader visual traditions and painterly languages informing her work.

Huitema’s paintings draw on a range of art-historical and visual references while maintaining a distinct internal coherence. The attenuated proportions and stylized poses of her figures recall traditions of early twentieth-century fashion illustration and Art Deco design, where gesture and embellishment echo the streamlined finesse of illustrators such as Erté and the theatrical poise found in interwar couture and stage design. Her compressed spaces also suggest affinities with aspects of Symbolist and Surrealist painting, in which shallow interiors and phantasmagoric backdrops function less as coherent environments than as psychological realms shaped by subconscious experience. Rather than aligning with a single historical framework, Huitema synthesizes these influences into a contemporary visual language that moves fluidly between illustration, painting, and cinematic staging. Working outside formal academic training, she has developed this vocabulary through sustained studio practice and close observation, resulting in a body of work that situates itself in dialogue with art history while remaining grounded in a self-directed approach to image making. In this context, Prussian Blue operates not only as a chromatic throughline but also as a conceptual one, binding together Huitema’s historical references and recurring motifs of protection and threat in constant tension.

Just in time for Halloween, John Kenn Mortensen talks dark fantasy, drawing by hand and bringing his distinctive illustrations to FLASK.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Halloween is the time to linger in the dark a little longer, and John Kenn Mortensen is the artist to guide you. His illustrations teem with grotesque creatures, scraggly line work, and unsettling oddballs: the kind of thing you glimpse out of the corner of your eye, then need to stare at and see more of.

“In the dark there are secrets and things to be explored,” he says as he explains his approach to the art and creature design you'll find in FLASK. “I see my work as a dark room, with a door slightly ajar at the end, where a little light comes in.”

That ajar door has made Mortensen a go-to name for the macabre. Now he’s opening it onto video games with FLASK, a dark fantasy roguelike deckbuilder from Chop Chop Games.

Inspired by Jim Henson’s 1986 cult classic Labyrinth and the thrash metal of Slayer, FLASK mixes gruesome fantasy, medieval imagery and black humour. Nightmarish creatures roam, magic is best handled with caution, and even a wizard has to worry about the mortgage on his tower.

For Mortensen, the leap meant taking his pen-and-paper illustrations digital, working with a team of artists to turn his monochrome creations into a playable world. That’s a big shift for an artist who has spent most of his career working solo across books, comics, animation, TV and exhibitions.

I caught up with Mortensen to talk about finding his visual identity, the music behind his monsters, and what it’s like to step into game development for the first time. And, of course, you can download FLASK on Steam this Halloween weekend (and beyond), and follow Mortensen on Instagram for more eerily good art.

Read the full Q&A with Mortensen below, and he's even shared a couple of new creatures coming to FLASK very soon.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

John Kenn Mortensen: It came from within. I have always been drawn to the dark; it is a much more interesting place to work. In the light everything is visible, revealed. In the dark there are secrets and things to be explored. I see my work as a dark room, with a door slightly ajar at the end, where a little light comes in.

JKM: Building on the gameplay mechanics Dario and Michael, co-founders and game developers at Chop Chop Games, already had, I focused on two things: the dark fantasy world of Labyrinth (the Jim Henson movie) and the sound and energy from Slayer (the band). From there, it just started to come alive.

JKM: It has been hard, and I don’t really know... it comes down to the art team; they are amazing to work with, and have been a huge support in bringing my monstrous creatures to life. On my side, I have mostly only worked with pen on paper, very old school.

JKM: Conveying the feelings in my art with colour has been a huge challenge, since most of my illustrations are in black and white. We have added lights, highlights, shadows, and colour, and it’s been really rewarding experimenting with what I’m comfortable with and seeing how we can add more depth when it comes to inserting my drawings into a digital format.

JKM: I tend to lose track of where ideas come from and how they morph into things in the process. But from the start, I wanted it to be dark fantasy mixed with medieval imagery. What’s even more special is that Labyrinth came out 40 years ago, and working on a project so inspired at the time of its anniversary is really rewarding.

JKM: This is my first time doing video games, so Chop Chop’s digital artists really played a huge role in this. First, gameplay had to come in and lay down the foundation, with auto-battler, roguelike, and theory crafting mechanics; then, thanks to the work with the artists, we were able to create a cohesive dark world over the framework of the game.

JKM: Mostly music. I listen to a lot of music. I have an hour every day where I will just walk and listen to music; that is where most of my ideas spring from.

JKM: Now, that is something I can’t take any credit for. We have had artists from outside, and artists on the team, create the card artwork. The rule for the artists working on the card art is that my visual style is the real world, and they have to see themselves as artists in that world and then create. It has been, and still is, a super fun process.

JKM: That, again, is credit to the art team, and it’s such a joy to have a team when I usually work solo. We have the best art team in the gaming world, I think. My art style is not something I have worked on in any direction; it has just sprung out of bad habits and laziness.

JKM: It has been a very different approach than I am used to, but I like that challenge. I always jump from one platform to another in my work: I have done TV shows, animation, live action, books, comics, art shows, and now video games. I see my working life as a big house with a lot of very different rooms where I can hang out and play with the people in them. The only thing I think about before entering is to be as honest and true to myself as possible. There are soooo many new ideas!

The amount of tax you owe on a real estate sale depends primarily on how long you held the property. This single factor — your holding period — determines whether you pay ordinary income tax rates or the lower long-term capital gains rates.

If you sell a property you have owned for one year or less, the profit is taxed as short-term capital gains at your ordinary income tax rate. For high earners, this can mean paying 32% to 37% federal tax on the gain, plus state income tax. Short-term gains are the most expensive way to realize real estate profits, which is why house flippers face a significantly higher tax burden than long-term investors.

These rates apply to taxable income after deductions, not gross income. Many FI retirees who have left traditional employment find themselves in the 0% or 15% long-term capital gains bracket — one of the most powerful tax advantages of early retirement.

In addition to the capital gains rate, high-income taxpayers owe an additional 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax on investment income (including real estate gains) when modified AGI exceeds $200,000 (single) or $250,000 (married filing jointly). This brings the maximum effective federal rate on long-term real estate gains to 23.8%.

Suppose you bought a rental property for $300,000, made $50,000 in improvements, and sold it for $500,000. Your gain is $150,000.

This is why timing matters enormously in real estate. Holding a property for just one additional day — crossing the one-year threshold — can save you tens of thousands of dollars.

The Section 121 exclusion is the single most valuable tax benefit in real estate. If you sell your primary residence and meet the ownership and use tests, you can exclude up to $250,000 in capital gains from taxation ($500,000 for married couples filing jointly). This is not a deduction — it is a complete exclusion. The gain simply does not exist for tax purposes.

To qualify, you must have owned AND used the home as your primary residence for at least 2 of the 5 years before the sale. The two years do not need to be consecutive. You can use this exclusion once every two years.

This rule creates powerful planning opportunities for FI-focused homeowners. If you bought a home, lived in it for two years, converted it to a rental for up to three years, and then sold it, you could still qualify for the exclusion because you used it as your primary residence for 2 of the past 5 years.

Your capital gain is not simply the sale price minus the purchase price. The IRS allows you to add several costs to your basis, which reduces your taxable gain.

Keep every receipt for capital improvements. A $35,000 kitchen remodel receipt from 2015 could save you $5,250 or more in capital gains tax when you sell.

Beyond the primary residence exclusion, several strategies allow real estate investors to reduce, defer, or eliminate capital gains tax on property sales.

A 1031 exchange allows you to sell an investment property and defer all capital gains tax by reinvesting the proceeds into a "like-kind" replacement property. The rules are strict:

A 1031 exchange does not eliminate the tax — it defers it. If you eventually sell the replacement property without doing another exchange, you owe tax on the accumulated gain from all prior exchanges. However, many investors execute a series of 1031 exchanges throughout their careers and eventually pass the properties to heirs, who receive a stepped-up basis that effectively eliminates the deferred gains.

If you have been depreciating a rental property (as required by the IRS), the depreciation you claimed is "recaptured" at sale and taxed at your ordinary income tax rate, up to a maximum of 25%. If your marginal tax rate is below 25% (for example, 12% or 22%), you pay that lower rate on the recaptured depreciation — the 25% is a ceiling, not a flat rate. This is separate from and in addition to regular capital gains tax.

Installment Sale (Section 453): Spread the gain over multiple years by receiving payments from the buyer over time. This can keep you in a lower tax bracket each year and is especially useful for large gains that would push you into the 20% capital gains bracket or trigger the 3.8% NIIT.

Opportunity Zone Investment: Invest capital gains into a Qualified Opportunity Zone Fund within 180 days of realizing the gain. You can defer the original gain until 2026 and potentially exclude gains on the new investment if held for 10+ years.

Convert to Primary Residence: If you own a rental property with significant appreciation, move into it and make it your primary residence for at least 2 years. You can then sell and use the Section 121 exclusion. Note: gains attributable to periods of non-qualified use (rental use after 2008) are not eligible for the exclusion.

Harvest Losses: If you have other investments with unrealized losses, sell them in the same year as your profitable real estate sale. Capital losses offset capital gains dollar-for-dollar, and up to $3,000 in excess losses can offset ordinary income.

Your cost basis includes every capital improvement you make to the property — new roof, HVAC replacement, kitchen remodel, bathroom addition, deck construction, and more. A $50,000 in documented improvements on a property held for 20 years can save you $7,500 to $10,000 in capital gains tax. Keep receipts, invoices, and before/after photos in a dedicated folder for each property. Routine repairs and maintenance do not count, but anything that adds value, prolongs life, or adapts the property to a new use qualifies as a capital improvement.

Follow these steps to determine your tax liability before selling.

Start with your original purchase price. Add closing costs from the purchase, all capital improvements made during ownership, and any assessments for local improvements. Subtract any depreciation claimed on rental property. The result is your adjusted basis.

Subtract your adjusted basis from the net sale price (sale price minus selling expenses like real estate commissions, transfer taxes, and closing costs). The result is your capital gain.

If the property was your primary residence and you lived in it for at least 2 of the past 5 years, exclude up to $250,000 ($500,000 married filing jointly) from the gain. If your gain is below the exclusion amount, you owe zero capital gains tax.

If you held the property for more than one year, long-term capital gains rates (0%, 15%, or 20%) apply based on your taxable income. If held for one year or less, short-term rates (your ordinary income tax rate) apply. Add 3.8% NIIT if your MAGI exceeds $200,000 single or $250,000 married.

If you claimed depreciation on a rental property, the total depreciation is recaptured and taxed at your ordinary income tax rate (up to a maximum of 25%) when you sell. Calculate this separately from the remaining capital gain, which is taxed at your applicable long-term capital gains rate.

An earlier version of this article stated that depreciation recapture is taxed at a flat 25% rate. The correct rule is that depreciation recapture is taxed at your ordinary income tax rate, up to a maximum of 25%. The article has been updated.

The most common way is the Section 121 primary residence exclusion. If you owned and lived in the home for at least 2 of the past 5 years, you can exclude up to $250,000 in gains ($500,000 for married couples). For gains exceeding the exclusion, strategies include installment sales to spread the gain over multiple tax years, opportunity zone investments to defer and potentially reduce the gain, or selling in a year when your other income is low to qualify for the 0% long-term capital gains rate.

Inherited property receives a "stepped-up basis" to the fair market value on the date of the decedent's death. This means if your parent bought a house for $100,000 and it was worth $400,000 when they died, your basis is $400,000 — not $100,000. If you sell for $410,000, your taxable gain is only $10,000. This stepped-up basis is one of the most significant tax benefits in the U.S. tax code.

If you claimed depreciation deductions on a rental property, the IRS "recaptures" that depreciation when you sell and taxes it at your ordinary income tax rate, up to a maximum of 25%. For example, if you depreciated $60,000 over your ownership period and your marginal tax rate is 25% or higher, you would owe $15,000 in depreciation recapture tax at sale (someone in the 12% bracket would owe $7,200 instead), in addition to any capital gains tax on the remaining profit. A 1031 exchange can defer depreciation recapture as well as capital gains.

No. A 1031 exchange applies only to property held for investment or business use. Your primary residence does not qualify. However, a hybrid strategy exists: convert your primary residence to a rental property, operate it as a rental for at least one to two years, then do a 1031 exchange into a new investment property. Consult a tax professional before attempting this, as the rules are complex.

It depends on your state. Most states tax capital gains as ordinary income. Nine states have no income tax (Alaska, Florida, Nevada, New Hampshire, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Washington, Wyoming), so no state capital gains tax applies. Some states like California tax capital gains at rates up to 13.3%. The state where the property is located and the state where you reside may both claim taxing authority.

You must own AND use the home as your primary residence for at least 2 out of the 5 years before the sale to qualify for the Section 121 exclusion. The 2 years do not need to be consecutive, and you can use this exclusion once every 2 years. Partial exclusions are available if you moved due to a change in employment, health, or certain unforeseen circumstances before meeting the 2-year requirement.

Capital gains tax on real estate can take a significant bite out of your profits — but the tax code provides powerful tools to reduce, defer, or eliminate it. The Section 121 exclusion ($250K single / $500K married) makes selling a primary residence tax-free for most homeowners. For investment properties, 1031 exchanges defer gains indefinitely, and strategies like installment sales, opportunity zones, and loss harvesting provide additional options. The key for FI-focused real estate investors is planning: track your cost basis meticulously, time your holding periods to qualify for long-term rates, and consult a tax professional before selling high-value properties. Real estate remains one of the most tax-advantaged asset classes when you understand and use the rules strategically.

#9092. How Former Theater Kid James Talarico Stands Up for the Arts in Texas

As Republicans exert an ever-tightening grip on creative freedom in the state, the Democratic Senate hopeful stands out for his track record on arts funding.

Every United States election season, a few candidates capture national attention. This year, one of those names is Democrat James Talarico, who is running for Senate against Republican Ken Paxton. A former theater kid turned language arts teacher now serving his fourth term in the Texas House of Representatives, Talarico would become the first Democrat elected US Senator since the 1980s if he wins.

Talarico has largely built his platform tackling education, a tough battle in a state that has seen eight school district takeovers since 2020. Among the bills he has co-authored is one that focuses on fine arts funding for public schools. Over the past years, the Texas arts scene has sat at the nexus between funding cuts and censorship.

First brought up in 2023 and subsequently reintroduced in 2025, the bill would have been the first of its kind in Texas, had it passed.

“This means hundreds of millions of dollars in new funding for music, dance, art, and theater programs! It’s a game changer,” Talarico, who has an endorsement from the Actors’ Equity Association, wrote on X in 2023. Hyperallergic has contacted Talarico’s campaign for comment.

Before earning his degrees in government and education, Talarico participated in his high school’s theater program, playing two leading roles: Danny Zuko in Grease and Aslan in The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe.

“Research shows fine arts programs improve student achievement, graduation rates, and mental health,” Talarico continued in his post. “I know it did for me when I was growing up.”

Austin-based artist Jean-Pierre Verdijo told Hyperallergic that he’s intrigued by Talarico’s overall message, which he views as focused on fair governance as opposed to fighting another party.

#9091. Molly Bounds "The Light That Loses, The Night That Wins" @ Mrs Gallery, Maspeth, NY

Mrs. is pleased to present The Light That Loses, The Night That Wins, Molly Bounds’ New York debut solo exhibition, on view at the gallery’s 6040 56th Drive location. This exhibition marks the Los Angeles-based artist’s second presentation with the gallery following The Armory Show in September 2025. The show will be on view through May 2, 2026.

Opening on the vernal equinox, a rare moment when the hours of daylight and night are equal, Molly Bounds offers light as the protagonist in her new series of paintings. It is versatile and ever-changing; it both conceals and reveals, and reminds us of the unrelenting forward movement of time. Depicting her subjects both in contemplation and in the midst of candid movement, Bounds continues her investigation into liminal moments where stillness and urgency shape the mood. Much like the transition from winter to spring, these figures appear on the threshold of a transformative shift.

There are also moments of escapism. In both It Sings in Me and Among of Green, Again a figure moves freely amongst rolling green hills, illuminated under the sun. The landscape appears bucolic and perhaps overly so - is this real or imagined? For Bounds this is less important; the ability to build optimism and a belief in renewal and rebirth is paramount. Contrasting with the scenes of pensive interiority, these landscapes communicate urgency, celebration, possibility, and fantasy. After the darkness of winter, spring wins.

It’s a lesson the whole creative industry needs to heed.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I'm in my fifties and far too old to use youth slang. But even I've come to realise that in recent years, the kids have started using "NPC", aka non-player character, as a term of ridicule for people in real life.

That makes sense, because typically in video games, the people who walk past you on the street are visual wallpaper. They give the impression that other humans are around, but they have no individuality.

This is exactly why the 2021 film Free Guy, in which Ryan Reynolds lives a repetitive, meaningless existence in a video game world, worked so well. We were all already in on the joke.

But now comes Grand Theft Auto 6, and its makers, Rockstar Games, are about to blow the concept of non-player characters right open.

In a cover feature for Edge, Creative Bloq's sister print magazine, the studio reveals it art-directed every one of the game’s NPCs, creating around 600,000 animations in the process.

Normally, procedural systems assemble background NPCs, making them largely interchangeable. Grand Theft Auto VI's non-player characters, however, will have their own personalities. Which means any Free Guy sequel (long mooted, but never confirmed) may have to rethink its premise entirely.

According to the Edge article, Rockstar set up a dedicated LA-based team of writers, directors and producers whose job was to make the pedestrians of Leonida, the game’s fictional take on Florida, feel individually realised.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

In practice, this means NPCs have personality traits that shape how they react to you. These include their temperament and aggression, where they are, what they’ve seen and how you’ve treated them. Different districts even have their own demographic and professional mix.

Rob Nelson, co-studio head at Rockstar North, describes a process of constantly asking how people might behave. “Who’s going to be aggressive? How many people will go for a weapon? How many are going to test me?”

Not only is this making me even more excited to play the game – even more excited than this brilliant GTA/South Park tie-in or these saucy GTA ads – it also says a lot about where we are as a culture. At a time when much of the creative industry is looking for faster, cheaper ways to fill digital worlds, Rockstar has done the opposite. And the rewards, I feel, will be immense.

We all talk endlessly about games being "immersive". But a city doesn’t feel real because of its landmarks. It feels real because of the passer-by who takes offence to something at precisely the wrong moment.

As D&AD’s AI & Creativity Report put it this year, AI has raised the floor, but not the ceiling. GTA 6 looks like an attempt to raise the ceiling the hard way, and I simply can't wait.

#9088. Nat Meade's "Franklin" @ HESSE FLATOW, NYC

HESSE FLATOW is pleased to announce the opening of Franklin, an exhibition of paintings and works on paper by Nat Meade, marking his third solo presentation with the gallery. The show is on view through April 18, 2026.

The emotional arc of life’s struggles and triumphs take shape within Meade’s figurative works, reflecting the artist’s everyday experiences as he navigates being a father, son, partner, and academic. Far from portraits of actual individuals, his protagonists mirror timeless archetypes. At times, we encounter a lone traveler searching for existential validation; at other times, we see through intergenerational dynamics. This allegorical distance via painting provides a realm for Meade to explore personal challenges through absurd, somber, and humorous tropes, while also furnishing a space rife with human nature that bears unequivocal resonance.

Meade’s reflections on his relationship with his father after his recent passing, and subsequent reevaluations of his own role as a parent percolate throughout the works in the exhibition. Vulnerability, pain, and mortality are themes Meade does not shy away from, yet the introduction of younger males in this body of work casts a sense of hope, acceptance, reconciliation, and renewal.

Faced with a pair of dangling legs from a cloud in Poise, we question whether a figure is ascending or descending from the heavens, a suggestion perhaps on the interchangeability of birth and death, be it physical or spiritual. Ghostly specters hover over certain individuals – a metaphor for inherited trauma and release. In the same way that a soul peels away from an expiring body in classic cartoons, we observe a spirit looking back on itself with what might be  happiness or regret. The exhibition’s title Franklin is a subtle nod to the 1974 horror film Texas Chainsaw Massacre, known for its portrayal of a deranged patriarchal family. Meade embraces this inner turmoil of contending with one’s violent and antagonistic impulses as his characters are visibly sublimated or put in their place. A vulture picking away at a corpse recalls the eternal punishment of Prometheus by Zeus, while a bearded figure on his hands and knees echoes William Blake’s portrayal of Nebuchadnezzar, condemned for his lust for power.

In contrast to the adults, Meade’s younger figures appear more harmonious. A young boy charts his own path as he steers a boat with a radiant torch, unclouded by societal and familial pressures. A sense of childlike wonder and adventure beholds an adolescent ankle-deep in a secluded cove, reaching in to touch the sea floor brilliantly covered in starfish, anemones, and mussels. In a related work, we observe two pairs of legs belonging to father and son in the same shallow pool, one tenderly guiding the other. Having in the past shown his figures wrestling with or victims of forces of nature, physically being overtaken by turbulent wind and crashing waves, Meade’s focus on calmer seas signals a turning point. He recognizes the need to acknowledge one’s rocky histories in order to heal and release future generations from similar burdens. Despite what may seem like an insurmountable heaviness, he reminds us of the stubborn resilience of human nature, making progress attainable.

#9087. French Galleries Accuse Art Basel Paris of "Disrespect, Even Contempt"

A group representing over a quarter of the exhibitors released a letter demanding compensation following the fair's abrupt closure.

Five days after Art Basel Paris announced it would prematurely terminate its 2026 edition on October 23, the Comité Professionnel des Galeries d’Art (CPGA), an industry group representing over a quarter of the fair's exhibitors, issued a letter demanding fair compensation and accusing event organizers of poor communication and mistreatment.

In the letter addressed to the new director of Art Basel Paris, Karim Crippa, the association demanded “concrete proposals for compensating exhibitors," stated that the galleries were never consulted about the event's early closure, and accused organizers of "disrespect, even contempt," according to Monopol. Along with CPGA President and Mon Charpentier gallery co-founder Philippe Charpentier, 14 members of the board signed the letter in support. The day after the association issued the letter, Crippa reportedly wrote to exhibitors promising a "concrete update in the coming days."

On October 22, event organizers for Art Basel Paris emailed exhibitors announcing that "in light of potential demonstrations across Paris this weekend and in the interest of safeguarding our visitors," the fair would close two days ahead of its planned October 25 end date. Following a temporary lockdown during installation at the Grand Palais on October 17, organizers proceeded with the original program before agreeing to end the fair early, citing the ongoing rallies over France’s failing education system and public services that have swept across the nation since mid-September.

#9086. Collectors Cristina Chacón and Diego Uribe to open contemporary art space in Miami

The new DC Lab, Miami Courtesy DC Art Foundation

The Colombian collectors and philanthropists Cristina Chacón and Diego Uribe will open DC Lab, a new contemporary art space on Miami’s Bird Road, expanding their nonprofit DC Art Foundation.

The admission-free, 9,000-sq.-ft space will host projects by international galleries that do not have a permanent presence in Miami, alongside research and public programming. Opening just in time for Miami Art Week on 29 November, DC Lab will present the first major survey in Miami of the Cuban artist Carlos Garaicoa, the foundation’s current artist in residence.

Based in Miami, Bogotá and Madrid, longtime partners Chacón and Uribe view collecting as a means of supporting the art community. “For us, collecting has always been more than acquiring works and has focused on a commitment to contributing to the cultural ecosystem,” Uribe tells The Art Newspaper.

The couple’s collection includes more than 500 Modern and contemporary works from around the globe, and they support institutions in Miami and beyond. At the Institute of Contemporary Art, Miami, they sit on the chairman’s council and the American and Latin American acquisitions boards. They also serve on the Museo Reina Sofía’s international patronage board and on the boards of Bogotá’s Museo de Arte Moderno and Miami’s Coral Gables Museum.

In 2021, the couple founded the DC Art Foundation to support artists and connect Miami’s art scene with the international community beyond Miami Art Week. Since 2022, the foundation has run a residency programme for mid-career and established artists.

“The foundation was a vehicle for the residency programme we fund at a private residence,” Uribe says. “The intention is to bring to Miami artists that activate the community, promoting local and international exchange.” Past residents include the Spanish textile artist Sonia Navarro and the Colombian artist Miler Lagos.

Carlos Garaicoa Photo: Oak Taylor Smith, courtesy DC Art Foundation

DC Lab will include exhibition and education spaces as well as a library. “This is a laboratory where experimental ideas and projects can happen in the city,” Uribe says. “We created a novel residency model that provides international galleries with space to present mid-career and established artists new to Miami, potentially inspiring them to settle here.”

Chacón adds that while international galleries often participate in Art Basel Miami Beach and its various satellite fairs, DC Lab will enable more in-depth projects. It will also strengthen the foundation’s community-centred work. “In our residency programme, artists commit to an educational activity, and we often organise talks,” she says. “But this new venue allows for deeper community engagement.”

The opening exhibition at DC Lab, co-presented with Italy’s Galleria Continua and Mor Charpentier (based in Paris and Bogotá), links the new venue to the residency. “While the residency programme runs independently from DC Lab, Garaicoa’s residency was especially fitting for the opening,” Chacón says.

Garaicoa—known for addressing cultural and political issues through architecture, urbanism and history—will present works from his November residency as well as other recent projects. “My residency work relates to Miami, its architecture and growth,” he says, “reflecting how politics and language coexist in architecture.”

Passion is the key driver for Chacón and Uribe’s new space. “We are not trying to be a museum,” Uribe says. “We continue being a private foundation supporting the local community.”

Chacón adds: “For us, art is an incurable disease that lifts the soul.”

Elmwood's Kyle Whybrow discusses the increasing hunger for tactile and intentional design.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As part of its 40th anniversary, Dolmio has revived its iconic puppet family. After a 10-year hiatus, the reintroduction of these familiar faces is both a return to tactile branding and a welcome nostalgia trip for fans.

Starring in some of the best adverts of the 2000s, the Dolmio family carries quite the legacy for the brand. In a world of social-first branding and AI slop advertising, Dolmio's return to form is an ingenious response to audiences that are growing increasingly hungry for human-led design.

To understand more about the Dolmio family's grand return, I caught up with Kyle Whybrow, ECD at Elmwood London, to understand the value of nostalgia and the art of reviving brand heritage.

The Dolmio brand and family were both born in Australia. Dolmio started life as a single bolognese sauce in a glass jar, and its success saw it grow into an established brand reaching wider markets, including the UK. Papa and Mama were originally cast as actors, then reimagined as handcrafted puppet characters in 2003, with the wider family joining them: Sophia, Carlo, Nina and Nico.

The idea behind them was simple and very human: the noisy, loving chaos of a family sitting down to eat together. In the UK, ‘When’s your Dolmio Day?’ turned a jar of sauce into a family ritual. They weren’t mascots bolted onto a product. They were the brand’s personality, given a face.

The puppets have grown up with the families watching them. The originals were definitely of their time, but our job wasn’t to replace them. It was to bring them into a modern family home, fit for today’s audience.

We gave each character clear principles, behaviours and visual codes, so each one has a distinct, contemporary personality. Then we built them into Dolmio’s wider identity, the red dot system, with real intent, so the family feels native to the brand’s graphic language rather than placed on top of it.

That system is consistent but flexible. One character can pop up inside the red dot, or the whole family can take the stage, whether that’s talking about the jar or sharing the moment over a bowl of pasta or a lasagne. That flexibility is what lets them stay culturally aware and show up in the moments that matter today. In the past they lived in a 30-second spot. Now they move between culture, content and commerce.

With respect, and a fine-tuned difference. We started by asking what made each character unmistakable, then amplified those details rather than diluting them. The silhouettes, the expressions and the family dynamic all stayed. Then we went deep on craft.

Every detail was considered and balanced: the subtle nuances in their features that feel familiar yet new, the clothing, the choice of material, the texture of their skin and hair, right down to the micro facial expressions and the wrinkles under the eyes. We took learnings from the great puppet and animation houses, because those tiny movements are what make a character feel alive and let people connect with them.

It was all about respecting where they came from while making them feel right for a modern audience. The red dot and the family make each other stronger: one gives instant recognition, the other gives people something to love. Fresh doesn’t have to mean new. Sometimes it just means sharper.

Nostalgia is a double-edged sword. Change too little, and you’re running a tribute act. Change too much, and you break the bond people have with these characters.

The other challenge was range and versatility across paid, shared, earned and owned. The same family had to deliver an emotional moment on TV, a shareable piece of culturally relevant content on social, and a clear reason to buy at the shelf. That meant building a proper system of rules, not one-off executions. Working closely with T&P was crucial here, so the family showed up consistently, whatever the channel or moment in the year.

Honestly, the invisible work. Anyone can bring back a much-loved character for a nostalgic moment. Building the principles, behaviours and codes that let a whole family perform consistently across every touchpoint is much harder.

I’m proud that each character feels truly distinct, yet they all clearly belong to Dolmio. And I love that they work as ambassadors as well as entertainers: they inspire people on social and still help convert them at the shelf. That’s design doing a commercial job as well as an emotional one.

I think audiences are hungry for craft and intent, and they can tell when it’s missing. The original Dolmio family were handmade puppets, and that tactile quality is a big part of why people love them.

You can’t buy decades of memory, but if you have it, it’s one of the most powerful distinctive assets a brand can own.

For the 40th, the family was rebuilt digitally, so we held every frame to the standard of the handmade originals. That’s why I don’t see it as analogue versus technology. Unreal Engine, motion capture, or the Puppetiser in Australia that lets families ‘puppetise’ themselves are brilliant when they serve the idea. Slop happens when the tool becomes the idea.

Because it’s earned. You can’t buy decades of memory, but if you have it, it’s one of the most powerful distinctive assets a brand can own. Nostalgia gives you instant recognition and connection, and it gives you permission to be playful. The trap is treating it as a rerun. Nostalgia works hardest when it bridges generations: parents who grew up with the Dolmio family get a smile of recognition, and their kids meet the characters for the first time and find them relevant now. It travels across markets too, because a family sitting down to eat needs no translation. That’s when nostalgia stops looking backwards and starts building the future.
